title: DIAGNOSTIC ALGORITHM AND TREATMENT FOR MICROSCOPIC COLITIS: A REVIEW.

subsections.content: Microscopic colitis (MC) is increasingly recognized as a common cause of chronic, nonbloody, watery diarrhea, particularly in older adults. Population-based studies have demonstrated a stable or rising incidence over recent decades, with age and female sex as consistent risk factors. A 9-year study in Olmsted County, Minnesota, reported an age- and sex-adjusted incidence of 21.0 cases per 100,000 person-years, with a marked female predominance (76.4% of cases) and a mean age at diagnosis of 65.8 years; collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis showed comparable but distinct incidence rates of 9.1 and 12.0 per 100,000 person-years, respectively ref [1]. Similarly, a nationwide Danish cohort from 2002 to 2011 observed a significant increase in diagnosed cases, with incidence rising to 24.7 per 100,000 inhabitants by 2011, largely attributable to heightened diagnostic awareness and increased biopsy rates ref [3]. The clinical presentation is typically characterized by chronic, intermittent diarrhea without blood, often accompanied by abdominal cramping and urgency, with symptoms most frequently emerging in the sixth decade of life ref [2]. Endoscopic findings are usually normal, necessitating histological confirmation via colonic biopsies for diagnosis ref [4].

Microscopic colitis (MC) encompasses two primary histological subtypes: collagenous colitis (CC) and lymphocytic colitis (LC), both characterized by chronic watery diarrhea in the absence of macroscopic mucosal abnormalities. The defining feature of CC is a thickened subepithelial collagen band (>10 μm), while LC is marked by an increased density of intraepithelial lymphocytes (>20 per 100 epithelial cells), often accompanied by lamina propria inflammation. These changes are typically patchy and may be more prominent in the distal colon, though biopsies from either the right or left colon demonstrate comparable diagnostic sensitivity, supporting the reliability of limited sampling protocols ref [5].

Emerging evidence suggests significant histological overlap between CC and LC, with up to 45% of CC cases showing elevated intraepithelial lymphocytes and 16% of LC cases exhibiting abnormal collagen deposition, challenging the traditional dichotomy and supporting the hypothesis that they represent a spectrum of the same underlying disease process ref [7]. Longitudinal studies reveal that histological abnormalities persist for at least one year in the majority of cases, with CC and LC showing greater persistence than incomplete MC (MCi), which may represent an early or resolving phase ref [6]. The pathophysiology involves immune-mediated epithelial injury, possibly triggered by bile acids, NSAIDs, or autoimmune mechanisms, leading to disrupted barrier function and altered fluid transport, though the precise sequence of events remains under investigation.

The diagnosis of microscopic colitis (MC) is frequently delayed due to its nonspecific clinical presentation, which overlaps significantly with functional bowel disorders such as diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) and functional diarrhea. This diagnostic ambiguity often leads to misdiagnosis and inappropriate management, as patients may undergo multiple evaluations before colonoscopic biopsy confirms MC. A systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated that nearly 39% of patients diagnosed with MC had prior or concurrent functional bowel disorder diagnoses, highlighting the substantial diagnostic overlap ref [8].

To address this challenge, clinical scoring systems have been developed to aid in pre-biopsy risk stratification. Kane et al. validated a scoring system incorporating age, sex, symptom duration, and medication use that effectively identifies patients at high risk for MC, thereby optimizing the selection of individuals for colonoscopy and targeted histology ref [9].

Emerging biomarkers offer non-invasive tools to differentiate MC from IBS. Fecal calprotectin (FC), measured by ELISA, is significantly elevated in active MC compared to IBS, providing a useful discriminant, though levels normalize in remission and are less reliable with rapid tests ref [10]. More recently, fecal eosinophil cationic protein (F-ECP) and eosinophil protein X (F-EPX) have shown promise as specific markers for collagenous colitis, correlating strongly with disease activity and treatment response, particularly during budesonide therapy ref [11] ref [12].

Microscopic colitis (MC) is increasingly recognized as a condition with significant associations with autoimmune and immune-mediated disorders. Studies have demonstrated a high prevalence of concomitant autoimmune diseases in MC patients, particularly collagenous colitis, with one multicenter Swedish study reporting that 30.2% of patients had at least one autoimmune condition, most commonly celiac disease (12.9%) and autoimmune thyroid disease (10.3%). These associations suggest a shared pathogenic immune dysregulation, with many autoimmune diagnoses preceding the onset of MC, indicating a potential underlying systemic autoimmune diathesis.

Beyond autoimmune comorbidities, pharmacological risk factors play a prominent role in MC pathogenesis. Concomitant use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) has been shown to significantly increase the risk of developing MC, with evidence suggesting a synergistic effect that may disrupt mucosal barrier integrity and immune homeostasis in the colon. This drug interaction represents one of the most modifiable risk factors in clinical practice.

Emerging evidence also points to rare but clinically significant associations between MC and systemic vasculitides. A recent study identified a markedly increased prevalence of MC in patients with Takayasu’s arteritis, with 67% of active TAK patients meeting MC diagnostic criteria compared to only 14% in inactive disease, suggesting a potential shared granulomatous or inflammatory pathway. These findings underscore the importance of screening for MC in patients with systemic autoimmune or inflammatory conditions presenting with chronic watery diarrhea.

Microscopic colitis is characterized by a chronic, relapsing-remitting clinical course, with symptoms often persisting for years despite treatment. Long-term studies reveal that even in clinical remission—defined as fewer than three stools per day—patients frequently experience residual symptoms such as abdominal pain, fatigue, arthralgia, and nocturnal defecation, significantly impairing health-related quality of life (HRQoL) compared to healthy controls ref [16]. These persistent symptoms underscore that clinical remission does not equate to full recovery, highlighting the substantial disease burden beyond stool frequency alone.

The development of a Microscopic Colitis Disease Activity Index (MCDAI) has provided a standardized tool to quantify symptom severity and disease activity prospectively, enabling more nuanced assessment of burden and treatment response ref [17]. Despite effective short-term induction therapy with budesonide, which achieves remission in up to 80% of patients, relapse rates are high after discontinuation, necessitating long-term management strategies that remain poorly defined ref [5].

The cumulative impact of chronic diarrhea, fecal incontinence, and systemic symptoms contributes to reduced work productivity, social withdrawal, and psychological distress, reinforcing microscopic colitis as a condition with significant, underappreciated morbidity. Although the risk of colorectal cancer is not elevated, the persistent symptom burden warrants ongoing clinical attention and patient-centered care models.

Collagenous colitis (CC) is characterized by a thickened subepithelial collagen band, typically measuring ≥10 μm, which lies beneath the surface epithelium of the colonic mucosa. This collagen deposition is the hallmark histological feature and is best visualized using Masson’s trichrome or Sirius red staining. The collagen band is often irregular, fragmented, or nodular in appearance and may be associated with surface epithelial injury, including flattening, vacuolization, or increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Inflammatory infiltrates in the lamina propria are usually mild to moderate and composed predominantly of lymphocytes and plasma cells, though neutrophils may be present in active disease.

Additional features include increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (often >20 per 100 epithelial cells), surface epithelial damage, and occasionally crypt architectural distortion. The collagen band is typically more prominent in the proximal colon but may be patchy, necessitating multiple biopsies for accurate diagnosis. Notably, the thickness of the collagen band may vary with disease activity and prior treatment, complicating interpretation in treated patients. The distinction between CC and lymphocytic colitis relies primarily on the presence of this collagenous layer, as both share overlapping inflammatory features ref [20]. The diagnostic criteria for CC remain histologically defined, with no validated serological or fecal biomarkers yet replacing endoscopic biopsy ref [19].

Lymphocytic colitis is characterized by an increased intraepithelial lymphocytosis (IELs) of ≥20 lymphocytes per 100 epithelial cells in the surface epithelium of the colonic mucosa, typically in the absence of significant crypt architectural distortion or inflammatory cell infiltration in the lamina propria. This hallmark feature distinguishes it from other forms of microscopic colitis and is often most prominent in the distal colon. The lymphocytes are predominantly CD3+ T cells, with a relative paucity of plasma cells and neutrophils, supporting a T-cell-mediated pathophysiology. The surface epithelium may show mild vacuolization or flattening, but crypt hyperplasia and goblet cell depletion are not consistent features. The lamina propria usually exhibits mild to moderate chronic inflammation, though this is not diagnostic by itself.

Differential diagnosis requires exclusion of celiac disease, infectious colitis, and drug-induced injury, as these may mimic lymphocytic colitis histologically. The presence of villous atrophy or crypt abscesses should prompt investigation for alternative etiologies. Notably, lymphocytic colitis may coexist with collagenous colitis in the same patient, suggesting a spectrum of disease rather than entirely distinct entities. Accurate diagnosis relies on adequate tissue sampling and careful histological evaluation, particularly in the context of chronic watery diarrhea in middle-aged to elderly individuals. The diagnostic criteria remain standardized across major pathology societies, with consensus emphasizing the quantitative assessment of IELs as the cornerstone of diagnosis ref [5].

subsections.subsection_title: Differential Diagnosis and Pitfalls in Histological Interpretation
subsections.content:
Differential diagnosis of microscopic colitis requires careful exclusion of other causes of chronic diarrhea with normal-appearing mucosa on colonoscopy, including celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), infectious colitis, and drug-induced mucosal injury. Histological features of collagenous and lymphocytic colitis may mimic early or mild IBD, particularly when crypt architectural distortion or increased intraepithelial lymphocytes are present, necessitating correlation with clinical context and serological testing. In celiac disease, villous atrophy and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes may overlap with lymphocytic colitis, but the involvement is typically proximal and accompanied by positive serology (e.g., tTG-IgA). Additionally, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use can induce subtle inflammatory changes that mimic microscopic colitis, requiring detailed medication history and, if possible, withdrawal trials. Pitfalls in interpretation include sampling error due to patchy involvement, inadequate biopsy depth (failure to capture the subepithelial collagen band in collagenous colitis), and overinterpretation of nonspecific lymphocytic infiltrates in the absence of strict diagnostic criteria.

Pathologists must also distinguish microscopic colitis from ischemic colitis, radiation colitis, and post-infectious colitis, which may show similar lymphocytic infiltration or collagen thickening but are typically associated with distinct clinical histories and topographic patterns. The use of standardized diagnostic criteria and scoring systems can reduce interobserver variability, though even experienced pathologists may misclassify cases without adequate clinical correlation. Ref [1] emphasizes that misdiagnosis rates remain significant in community practice due to lack of awareness and inconsistent biopsy protocols, underscoring the need for multidisciplinary collaboration between gastroenterologists and pathologists to optimize diagnostic accuracy.

First-line pharmacologic therapy for microscopic colitis focuses on symptom control, particularly for patients with moderate to severe watery diarrhea. Budesonide, a non-systemic glucocorticoid with high first-pass metabolism, is the most evidence-supported agent, demonstrating superior efficacy over placebo in inducing clinical and histological remission in both collagenous and lymphocytic colitis. According to the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) guidelines, budesonide 9 mg/day for 8 weeks is recommended as the initial pharmacologic intervention due to its favorable benefit-risk profile and low systemic absorption, minimizing long-term steroid-related adverse effects ref [22].

For patients who are intolerant or unresponsive to budesonide, or in cases where it is contraindicated, cholestyramine may be considered as an alternative first-line option, particularly if bile acid malabsorption is suspected. The AGA technical review supports its use based on modest but consistent evidence from randomized trials, especially in patients with diarrhea-predominant symptoms ref [3]. Anti-diarrheal agents such as loperamide are often used adjunctively for mild symptoms or as bridge therapy, though they lack robust evidence for inducing remission and are not recommended as monotherapy. The AGA guidelines emphasize that treatment goals should prioritize symptom resolution and quality of life improvement, given the benign long-term prognosis of microscopic colitis and absence of increased cancer risk.

For patients with microscopic colitis who fail to respond to first-line budesonide or bismuth subsalicylate, second-line pharmacologic options include systemic corticosteroids, immunomodulators such as azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, and anti-tumor necrosis factor (anti-TNF) agents. Although evidence is limited, case series and retrospective analyses suggest that azathioprine may induce remission in steroid-dependent or refractory cases, particularly in patients with persistent inflammation despite initial therapy. Anti-TNF agents like infliximab have shown efficacy in small cohorts, especially in patients with concomitant autoimmune conditions or severe, debilitating symptoms unresponsive to conventional therapies. Notably, older age at diagnosis has been associated with improved response to bismuth subsalicylate, suggesting potential heterogeneity in treatment pathways that may inform individualized approaches in refractory disease ref [24].

Dietary interventions, including elimination of caffeine, lactose, or gluten, may be considered adjunctively in refractory cases, particularly when comorbid celiac disease or food sensitivities are suspected. In select patients, cholestyramine has been used to manage bile acid malabsorption contributing to persistent diarrhea. Emerging data support the potential role of fecal microbiota transplantation in refractory microscopic colitis, though large-scale trials are lacking. Close monitoring for disease recurrence and long-term complications remains essential, as refractory disease often correlates with prolonged symptom burden and reduced quality of life.

subsections.subsection_title: Role of Dietary and Lifestyle Modifications
subsections.content:
Dietary and lifestyle modifications play a supportive, though not definitively curative, role in the management of microscopic colitis. While no specific dietary components—such as protein, carbohydrates, fiber, or fatty acids—have been consistently linked to disease development or exacerbation, strong evidence implicates smoking and alcohol consumption as modifiable risk factors. A large population-based cohort study found that smoking confers a more than twofold increased risk of microscopic colitis (HR: 2.29), while high alcohol intake showed a trend toward increased risk (HR: 1.89 for highest quartile), suggesting these behaviors may influence mucosal inflammation through immune or barrier-disrupting mechanisms ref [25]. Notably, alcohol intake appeared to attenuate the smoking-related risk in post hoc analysis, hinting at complex interactions between environmental exposures ref [25].

Although no standardized dietary regimen is recommended for microscopic colitis, clinical experience suggests that patients may benefit from eliminating potential irritants such as caffeine, lactose, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which are known to exacerbate diarrhea. Lifestyle interventions, particularly smoking cessation, are strongly encouraged as a first-line adjunct to pharmacologic therapy, given the robust association between tobacco use and disease incidence. Weight management and stress reduction, while not directly studied in MC cohorts, are often advised based on their general benefits in inflammatory bowel conditions and their potential to modulate gut-brain axis activity.

subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Implications of the Diagnostic Algorithm
subsections.content:
The diagnostic algorithm for microscopic colitis (MC) has profound clinical implications, particularly in distinguishing it from functional bowel disorders and other causes of chronic non-bloody diarrhea. Accurate diagnosis hinges on obtaining adequate colonic biopsies from multiple sites, as histopathological features may be patchy and easily missed without systematic sampling. Failure to implement this algorithm can lead to misdiagnosis as irritable bowel syndrome, resulting in delayed or inappropriate therapy. The algorithm’s emphasis on histology over endoscopic appearance underscores the necessity of pathologist involvement, as endoscopic findings are typically normal in MC. Ref [1] highlights that adherence to standardized biopsy protocols significantly improves diagnostic yield and reduces diagnostic delays, particularly in regions with low clinical awareness. Furthermore, integrating clinical context—such as medication use (e.g., PPIs, NSAIDs) and autoimmune comorbidities—enhances diagnostic specificity and guides targeted investigations.

The diagnostic algorithm also informs prognostic stratification and therapeutic decision-making. Patients diagnosed early through a structured approach are more likely to respond to first-line therapies such as budesonide, whereas delayed diagnosis often correlates with prolonged symptom burden and reduced quality of life. Emerging evidence supports the inclusion of biomarkers, such as fecal calprotectin, as adjuncts to rule out inflammatory bowel disease, though they cannot replace histology. Standardizing the diagnostic pathway across institutions can reduce variability in care and improve population-level outcomes, particularly as MC prevalence continues to rise globally.

subsections.subsection_title: Current Treatment Guidelines and Evidence Base
subsections.content:
Current treatment guidelines for microscopic colitis emphasize stepwise pharmacologic intervention, beginning with budesonide as first-line therapy for both collagenous and lymphocytic colitis due to its superior efficacy and favorable safety profile compared to systemic corticosteroids. Refractory cases may require second-line agents such as cholestyramine, mesalamine, or anti-TNF agents, though evidence for these is less robust and often derived from small cohort studies. Recent meta-analyses support the use of budesonide for inducing remission, with response rates exceeding 80% in randomized trials, while highlighting the high relapse rate upon discontinuation, necessitating maintenance strategies in select patients. Dietary modifications, particularly avoidance of NSAIDs and proton pump inhibitors, are increasingly recognized as critical adjuncts to pharmacotherapy, given their established role in disease induction and exacerbation.

Emerging evidence suggests that microbiome-targeted therapies, including fecal microbiota transplantation, hold promise but remain investigational. The American Gastroenterological Association recommends individualized treatment based on disease severity, comorbidities, and drug exposure history, with close monitoring for symptom recurrence and quality of life outcomes. Long-term follow-up data underscore the importance of a multidisciplinary approach integrating gastroenterology, pathology, and nutrition to optimize therapeutic outcomes.

The authors gratefully acknowledge the contributions of pathologists and gastroenterologists whose meticulous histological and clinical work have advanced the understanding of microscopic colitis. We thank the researchers behind the development of standardized diagnostic criteria and disease activity indices, which have enabled more consistent patient stratification and outcome assessment across multicenter studies.

We also recognize the pivotal role of patient advocacy groups and longitudinal cohort initiatives that have facilitated the collection of real-world data on disease progression and treatment response, particularly in underrepresented populations. The insights derived from these efforts have been instrumental in shaping contemporary clinical algorithms.
